title: Floquet dressing of bulk metallic bands in 2H-NbSe2
authors: Cong Li, Qirui Cui, Maciej Dendzik, Magnus H. Berntsen, Wanyu Chen, Zhilin Li, Anna Delin, Wentao Zhang, Oscar Tjernberg
abstract: Floquet dressing offers a route to controlling electronic states through periodic optical driving. Its realization in solids has centred primarily on topological-insulator surface states, semiconductors and two-dimensional Dirac semimetals. Extending this control to bulk metals would enable manipulation of the itinerant states underlying metallic transport and collective order. Yet strong screening and rapid scattering have long cast doubt on its feasibility in bulk metals, while photoelectron dressing complicates its identification. Here we identify Floquet dressing of the overlapping, bulk-derived metallic bands of 2H-NbSe2 using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Photon-shifted replicas in a sparse unoccupied-state window retain the parent-band dispersions and appear only during pump--probe overlap. Rotating the pump's linear polarization at fixed probe polarization redistributes replica weight between momentum-space branches. With a common parameter set, a model accounting for the optical fields inside and outside the solid captures this redistribution through coherent Floquet--Volkov interference more closely than either pathway alone or their incoherent intensity sum. These findings extend Floquet dressing to the itinerant bulk bands of a multiband metal without relying on the observation of energy gaps opened by hybridization between parent bands and their photon-dressed replicas, providing a basis for exploring how coherent optical dressing couples to metallic transport and collective electronic phases.
summary: This work reports the observation of Floquet dressing in the bulk metallic bands of 2H-NbSe2 using time-resolved ARPES. By analyzing polarization-dependent sideband replicas, the authors demonstrate that the observed signal is best explained by a coherent interference model combining initial-state and final-state dressing effects. This extends the utility of Floquet engineering to bulk metallic conductors.
main_problem: The study aims to extend the control of electronic states via Floquet dressing from surface states to the itinerant bulk bands of metals.
main_result: The authors successfully identify Floquet dressing in the bulk metallic bands of 2H-NbSe2, showing that the coherent Floquet-Volkov interference model best describes the observed momentum-space weight redistribution.
method: The research combines time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (tr-ARPES) experiments with detailed theoretical modeling of coherent Floquet-Volkov interference.
model_or_system: The physical system is 2H-NbSe2, a layered multiband metal. The theoretical framework models the dressing effect using both initial-state (Bloch) and final-state (Volkov) approximations, calculating the total intensity via coherent interference.
key_observables: Photon-shifted replicas in the unoccupied state window, polarization-dependent redistribution of replica weight, and momentum distribution curves (MDCs).
important_parameters: Pump photon energy ($\hbar\omega_{	ext{pump}} = 1.2$ eV), probe energy (18 eV), and polarization angles ($\phi$).
main_assumptions: The initial-state contribution must be separated from final-state photoemission effects, and the analysis relies on comparing coherent interference against incoherent sums.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate time-delay dependence separating field-synchronous signals, constant-energy contours showing replica structure, and MDC comparisons validating the coherent interference model over incoherent sums.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the feasibility of the measurement using tr-ARPES, then using polarization dependence and MDC analysis to distinguish between initial-state and final-state dressing, culminating in a detailed theoretical comparison between coherent and incoherent interference models.
why_interesting: The ability to observe and model coherent optical dressing in bulk metals, rather than just surface states, opens a new avenue for controlling metallic transport and collective electronic phases using light.
